steps.stepTitle: Scene 1: Change the Outfit, Keep the Meaning!
steps.settingDescription: Inside a hall of refracting mirrors, Maharaj Vakya tests whether sentences can change clothes—affirmative to negative, simple to complex, or real to hypothetical—without changing their core truth!

dialogues.line: Transform 'Everyone loves honesty' into a negative sentence WITHOUT flipping its meaning! If you write 'Everyone hates honesty', the alarm rings!
Aha! Watch this: 'There is NO ONE who does NOT love honesty!' Same truth, brand-new negative clothes!

Bravo, Chikoo! Transformation of Sentences reshapes grammar—affirmative/negative, interrogative/assertive, parts of speech, simple/compound/complex, and conditional/concessive clauses—while preserving exact meaning.
And inside Conditional mirrors, watch the tense locks! Zero, First, Second, and Third Conditionals refuse 'will' or 'would' inside the 'if'-clause!

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Transform sentences across structure and part of speech while preserving meaning, and master all four Conditional types.

steps.stepTitle: Discover: Affirmative/Negative, Parts of Speech & Clause Synthesis
steps.subtopicTitle: Preserving Meaning Across Structure & Part-of-Speech Shifts
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Sentence Transformation is grammar origami: fold the same sheet ('He was too tired to run') into a crane ('He was so tired that he could not run')—new shape, exact same message!
steps.formalDefinition: Transformation of sentences converts a clause from one grammatical structure to another (affirmative ↔ negative, assertive ↔ interrogative/exclamatory, simple ↔ compound ↔ complex, or shifting a word's part of speech) without altering its proposition.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Master the five most tested Class IX–X transformations:
1) Affirmative ↔ Negative (keep meaning!): 'Only + X' → 'None but + X' ('Only the brave win' = 'None but the brave win'); 'Always' → 'Never + antonym' ('Always speak the truth' = 'Never tell a lie'); 'As soon as...' → 'No sooner had/did ... than...'; 'Too... to' → 'So... that + cannot/could not'.
2) Assertive ↔ Interrogative (rhetorical): 'Everyone knows him' ↔ 'Who does not know him?'. Exclamatory ↔ Assertive: 'What a vibrant mural this is!' ↔ 'This is a very vibrant mural.'
3) Part-of-Speech Conversion: 'He listened with patience' (Noun) ↔ 'He listened patiently' (Adverb); 'She succeeded' (Verb) ↔ 'She was successful' (Adjective) ↔ 'She achieved success' (Noun).
4) Simple ↔ Compound ↔ Complex: 'In spite of his illness' (Simple prep phrase) ↔ 'He was ill, yet he attended' (Compound) ↔ 'Although he was ill, he attended' (Complex).

structurePatterns.formula: Only → None but | As soon as → No sooner... than | Must → Cannot but V1 | Too... to → So... that
structurePatterns.sample: As soon as the rain stopped, we left. = No sooner did the rain stop than we left.

structurePatterns.formula: In spite of / Despite + NP/V-ing (Simple) | ... yet/but ... (Compound) | Although/Though ... (Complex)
structurePatterns.sample: Despite the mist, we hiked. = It was misty, yet we hiked. = Although it was misty, we hiked.

realLifeExamples.sentence: She could not help smiling at Chikoo's rhyme. ↔ She could not but smile at Chikoo's rhyme.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Both mean 'She had to smile' ('cannot help + V-ing' vs. 'cannot but + Bare V1').

realLifeExamples.sentence: He answered every question with confidence. ↔ He answered every question confidently.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Assertive 'Everybody respects courage' transformed to negative: 'Nobody respects courage.'
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: There is nobody who does not respect courage.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: 'Nobody respects courage' reverses the meaning! Use a balanced negative ('There is nobody who does not...') to preserve meaning.

exceptions: 'Unless' (Complex) transforms cleanly to Compound 'or / otherwise': 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the train' = 'Hurry up, or you will miss the train.'

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 1: Keep the Meaning in Negative Clothes
steps.storyPrompt: Maharaj Vakya challenges you inside the Transformation Mirror: "Only skilled navigators can cross this channel."
steps.questionPrompt: Transform this into a NEGATIVE sentence WITHOUT changing its meaning:
options: Skilled navigators cannot cross this channel.
None but skilled navigators can cross this channel.
No skilled navigators can cross this channel.
Not only skilled navigators can cross this channel.
acceptedAnswers: None but skilled navigators can cross this channel.
steps.hint: What negative pair always replaces 'Only + [person/group]' without altering meaning?
steps.feedbackCorrect: Maharaj Vakya: "Mirror passed! 'None but' preserves 'Only' with negative grammar cleanly."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Use 'None but...' (meaning 'nobody except...') to keep the exact meaning of 'Only...'.

feedbackWrongByOption.Skilled navigators cannot cross this cha: Completely flips the truth of the sentence!
feedbackWrongByOption.Not only skilled navigators can cross th: Means unskilled people can cross too—changes meaning!

steps.simplerExample: Only hard work brings mastery. → Nothing but hard work brings mastery.

steps.subtopicTitle: Transforming Part of Speech & Clause Structure
steps.storyPrompt: Vaani transforms: "Although the mountain path was slippery, the scouts climbed steadily." into a Simple Sentence: "____ the slippery mountain path, the scouts climbed steadily."
steps.questionPrompt: Type the one-word preposition that converts 'Although + clause' into a Simple Sentence:
steps.sentenceTemplate: ________ the slippery mountain path, the scouts climbed steadily.
steps.hint: One word (NOT 'In spite of', which is three words—and NEVER *Despite of!)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Exact! 'Despite + Noun Phrase' replaces 'Although + Clause' cleanly (and never add 'of' after 'Despite')."
steps.simplerExample: Although it rained, we played. → Despite the rain, we played.

steps.subtopicTitle: Zero, First, Second, Third & Inverted Conditionals
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: The 'If'-Clause is a strict no-'will'/no-'would' zone! Keep 'will' and 'would' ONLY on the Result side of the fence: First Conditional = [If + Present] → [will + V1]; Second = [If + Past / were] → [would + V1]; Third = [If + had + V3] → [would have + V3]!
steps.formalDefinition: Conditional structures link a condition clause (protasis, typically introduced by 'if' or 'unless') with a result clause (apodosis). English distinguishes Zero (universal facts), First (real future possibility), Second (unlikely/imaginary present or future), and Third (impossible/unfulfilled past) conditionals according to tense pairing.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Memorise the four Conditional ladders completely:
0) Zero Conditional (Always true / Science): If + Simple Present → Simple Present ('If you heat ice, it melts').
1) First Conditional (Real future possibility): If + Simple Present → will / can / may + V1 ('If you study hard, you will pass'—NEVER *If you will study hard!).
2) Second Conditional (Imaginary / Hypothetical now): If + Simple Past (use 'WERE' for all subjects formally: 'If I were you...') → would / could + V1 ('If I had wings, I would fly').
3) Third Conditional (Regret / Unfulfilled Past): If + Past Perfect ('had + V3') → would / could / might + have + V3 ('If she had caught the early bus, she wouldn't have missed the bell').
Formal Inversion: You may omit 'if' in Second/Third conditionals by inverting: 'Were I the king...' (= If I were) and 'Had I known...' (= If I had known).

structurePatterns.formula: 0: Pres → Pres | 1st: Pres → will+V1 | 2nd: Past/were → would+V1 | 3rd: had+V3 → would have+V3
structurePatterns.sample: If it rains, plants grow (0) • will stay (1) • had/would fly (2) • had trained/would have won (3).

structurePatterns.formula: Had + Subject + V3, Subject + would have + V3
structurePatterns.sample: Had the watchman checked the lock, the key would not have vanished.

realLifeExamples.sentence: If I were the stadium captain, I would schedule extra practice on Saturday morning.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Second Conditional uses subjunctive 'were' (even after 'I/he/she') + 'would + V1'.

realLifeExamples.sentence: Had Chikoo read the sign carefully, he would not have stepped onto wet paint.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Inverted Third Conditional (= 'If Chikoo had read...') paired with 'would not have + V3'.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: If it will rain tomorrow, we cancel the match; and if he would have called me, I would go.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the match; and if he had called me, I would have gone.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Never place 'will' or 'would have' inside the 'if'-clause—keep Simple Present in First Conditional and 'had + V3' in Third Conditional.

exceptions: 'Provided (that)', 'on condition that', and 'as long as' work like strong 'if' in First/Zero conditionals ('You may borrow the scroll provided that you return it by Friday').

steps.storyPrompt: Detective Ira reflects on an earlier clue: "If the courier had taken the river ferry, he ____ arrived on time."
steps.questionPrompt: Type the two missing Third-Conditional words ('____ ____'):
steps.sentenceTemplate: If the courier had taken the river ferry, he ________ arrived on time.
steps.hint: Condition has Past Perfect ('had taken') → Result before V3 ('arrived') takes 'would ____'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Exact Third Conditional! 'If + had + V3' pairs strictly with 'would/could/might have + V3'."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Use 'would have' (or 'could have') before 'arrived' to match 'had taken'.
steps.simplerExample: If she had left earlier, she would have caught the train.

steps.storyPrompt: Chikoo tests a mirror riddle: "If I will find a magic lamp, I would ask for endless mangoes!"
steps.questionPrompt: Pick the grammatically consistent SECOND Conditional (unreal present/future dream):
options: If I found a magic lamp, I would ask for endless mangoes!
If I find a magic lamp, I would ask for endless mangoes!
If I would find a magic lamp, I will ask for endless mangoes!
If I had found a magic lamp, I would ask for endless mangoes!
acceptedAnswers: If I found a magic lamp, I would ask for endless mangoes!
steps.hint: Second Conditional (imaginary dream) pairs 'If + Simple Past (found)' with 'would + V1 (would ask)'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Dreamy and grammatical! Second Conditional pairs Simple Past 'found' with 'would ask' (zero 'will/would' inside 'If')."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Match 'would ask' in the result clause with Simple Past 'found' inside the 'if'-clause.

feedbackWrongByOption.If I find a magic lamp, I would ask for: Mixes First Conditional ('find') with Second Conditional ('would ask')!

steps.simplerExample: If I won a telescope, I would study Saturn every night.

steps.settingDescription: All four transformation mirrors shimmer in harmony—affirmative to negative, simple to complex, and every conditional locked cleanly.

dialogues.line: Had you not trained so diligently, this chamber would never have unlocked so swiftly! Look—an inverted Third Conditional!

summaryRules.heading: Meaning-Preserving Sentence Transformations
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Transform sentences without flipping truth: 'Only' ↔ 'None but'; 'Too... to' ↔ 'So... that + cannot/could not'; 'In spite of / Despite + NP' (Simple) ↔ 'Although + Clause' (Complex) ↔ '..., yet/but ...' (Compound).
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: As soon as S + V ... ↔ No sooner did/had S + V ... than ...
summaryRules.example: He was too proud to apologise. ↔ He was so proud that he could not apologise.

summaryRules.heading: Changing Parts of Speech Without Losing Meaning
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Swap verbs, nouns, adjectives, and adverbs cleanly: 'spoke with pride' (Noun) = 'spoke proudly' (Adverb) = 'was proud' (Adjective).

summaryRules.heading: All Four Conditionals (Never Put 'will/would' in 'If'-Clause!)
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Zero: Pres → Pres. First: Pres → will+V1. Second: Past / were → would+V1. Third: had+V3 → would have+V3. Inverted: 'Were I...', 'Had I known...'.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: 0: Pres/Pres | 1: Pres/will V1 | 2: Past/would V1 | 3: had V3/would have V3
summaryRules.example: Had we left earlier, we would have seen the sunrise.

memoryAids: Grammar Origami: fold a sentence into a new shape (Simple / Complex / Negative / Interrogative), yet keep the exact same message inside!
No-'Will' Fence: 'will' and 'would' stay on the Result side—NEVER inside the 'If'-clause!

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: If you will practise daily, you would improve; and despite of the rain we played.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: If you practise daily, you will improve; and despite the rain we played.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Drop 'will' from the 'if'-clause, align First Conditional ('will improve'), and never put 'of' after 'despite'.

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: Had I knew the truth earlier, I would help you yesterday.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: Had I known the truth earlier, I would have helped you yesterday.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Inverted Third Conditional uses Past Participle V3 ('known') after 'Had', paired with 'would have + V3'.

exceptions: Note the difference between 'cannot help + V-ing' ('She cannot help laughing') and 'cannot but + Bare V1' ('She cannot but laugh').
Formal Second Conditional uses 'were' for all persons ('If she were present...').
textbookNotes: Grounded in Assam Ch. 3 & Ch. 16 (Transformation of Sentences) and Ch. 7 (Clauses: conditional/concessive transformation).

questions.questionText: Transform without changing meaning: "The riddle was too intricate for Chikoo to solve."
options: The riddle was so intricate that Chikoo could solve it.
The riddle was so intricate that Chikoo could not solve it.
The riddle was very intricate that Chikoo cannot solve it.
The riddle was enough intricate for Chikoo to solve.
questions.explanation: Past 'was too + Adj + for X to V1' transforms to 'was so + Adj + that + X + could not + V1 (+ it)'.
distractorRationales: Correct: 'so intricate that Chikoo could not solve it'.
Uses 'very' instead of 'so' and mismatches tense 'cannot'.
questions.grammarRule: Transform 'too + Adj + to V1' into 'so + Adj + that + S + cannot/could not + V1'.

questions.questionText: Convert into an Assertive (Declarative) sentence: "What a melodious song Vaani sang!"
options: Did Vaani sing a melodious song?
Vaani sang a very melodious song.
Vaani sang a what melodious song.
Vaani did not sing a melodious song.
questions.explanation: 'What a + Adj + Noun + S + V!' becomes 'S + V + a + very + Adj + Noun.'
questions.grammarRule: Convert 'What a / How' exclamations to assertive sentences using intensifiers like 'very' or 'great'.

questions.questionText: Transform into a rhetorical Interrogative sentence preserving the exact same meaning: "Nobody can forget Dr. Kalam's inspiring words."
options: Can nobody forget Dr. Kalam's inspiring words?
Who can ever forget Dr. Kalam's inspiring words?
Who cannot forget Dr. Kalam's inspiring words?
Did everyone forget Dr. Kalam's inspiring words?
questions.explanation: A negative assertive statement ('Nobody can...') turns into a positive rhetorical question ('Who can ever...?') implying the answer 'Nobody!'.
distractorRationales: Awkward double force; 'Anybody' or 'Who' is standard.
Correct: positive rhetorical question matches negative statement.
questions.grammarRule: Negative assertive ('Nobody...') ↔ Positive rhetorical question ('Who...?'); Positive assertive ('Everyone...') ↔ Negative rhetorical question ('Who does not...?').

questions.questionText: Rewrite "The team celebrated its victory with enthusiasm" replacing the noun 'enthusiasm' with an ADVERB:
options: The team celebrated its victory enthusiastic.
The team celebrated its victory enthusiastically.
The team was enthusiastic about celebrating its victory.
The enthusiastic team celebrated its victory.
questions.explanation: 'With enthusiasm' (preposition + noun) converts cleanly to the single adverb 'enthusiastically' modifying 'celebrated'.
distractorRationales: 'Enthusiastic' is an adjective, not an adverb.
questions.grammarRule: Prepositional phrases of manner ('with + abstract noun') transform directly into '-ly' adverbs.

questions.questionText: Convert the Complex sentence "If you follow the safety rules, you will avoid accidents" into a COMPOUND sentence:
options: Following the safety rules helps avoid accidents.
Follow the safety rules, and you will avoid accidents.
Because you follow the safety rules, you avoid accidents.
Unless you follow the safety rules, you will face accidents.
questions.explanation: 'Follow the safety rules, and you will avoid accidents' joins two independent clauses with coordinating 'and' (Compound).
distractorRationales: Correct: Compound sentence (Imperative clause + 'and' + Main clause).
questions.grammarRule: 'If + positive condition' (Complex) becomes '[Imperative], and...' (Compound); 'Unless' becomes '[Imperative], or...'.

questions.questionText: Complete this Zero Conditional (scientific fact): "If water reaches 0 degrees Celsius, it ____."
options: would freeze
freezes
froze
had frozen
questions.explanation: Zero Conditional expresses invariable natural laws with Simple Present in BOTH clauses ('reaches' → 'freezes').
questions.grammarRule: Zero Conditional: If + Simple Present, Simple Present (general/scientific truths).

questions.questionText: Choose the accurate First Conditional sentence:
options: If the courier will arrive before noon, we will open the vault.
If the courier arrives before noon, we will open the vault.
If the courier arrived before noon, we will open the vault.
If the courier arrives before noon, we would open the vault.
questions.explanation: First Conditional uses Simple Present ('arrives') in the 'if'-clause and 'will + V1' ('will open') in the result clause.
questions.grammarRule: First Conditional: If + Simple Present, will/can/may + V1.

questions.questionText: Complete this unreal present/hypothetical advice: "If I ____ you, I ____ accept the captaincy cheerfully."
options: am / would
were / would
was / will
had been / would
questions.explanation: Second Conditional uses subjunctive 'were' ('If I were you') paired with 'would + V1' ('would accept').
questions.grammarRule: Second Conditional: If + Simple Past / subjunctive 'were', would/could + V1.

questions.questionText: Complete this impossible-past reflection: "If Dev ____ the compass earlier, the scouts wouldn't have lost the trail."
options: checked
would have checked
had checked
has checked
questions.explanation: 'Wouldn't have lost' signals a Third Conditional, requiring Past Perfect ('had checked') in the 'if'-clause.
distractorRationales: Simple Past pairs with 'wouldn't lose', not 'wouldn't have lost'.
Correct: 'If + had + V3' pairs with 'wouldn't have + V3'.
Present Perfect does not match past unfulfilled result.
questions.grammarRule: Third Conditional: If + had + V3, would/could/might + have + V3.

questions.questionText: Rewrite "If you had informed the watchman, he would have unlocked the side gate" WITHOUT using 'if':
options: Did you inform the watchman, he would have unlocked the side gate.
Had you informed the watchman, he would have unlocked the side gate.
Have you informed the watchman, he would have unlocked the side gate.
Were you informed the watchman, he would have unlocked the side gate.
questions.explanation: Omit 'if' in a Third Conditional by moving 'Had' ahead of the subject ('Had you informed...').
distractorRationales: Cannot use 'Did' for Third Conditional inversion.
Changes meaning to passive 'Were you informed'.
questions.grammarRule: Invert Third Conditionals by dropping 'if' and placing 'Had' before the subject.

questions.subtopicTitle: Complex to Simple with 'so that' → 'in order to'
questions.questionText: Convert "We planted neem trees so that we might shade the courtyard" into a SIMPLE sentence (one finite verb):
options: We planted neem trees because we wanted shade in the courtyard.
We planted neem trees in order to shade the courtyard.
We planted neem trees, so the courtyard got shade.
Planting neem trees, the courtyard was shaded.
questions.explanation: 'So that + clause' (Complex purpose) condenses into an infinitive phrase of purpose 'in order to / to + V1' (Simple sentence with only one finite verb 'planted').
distractorRationales: Correct: Simple sentence using 'in order to + V1'.
questions.grammarRule: Convert 'so that + S + may/might + V1' (Complex) to 'in order to / to + V1' (Simple).

questions.questionText: Which pair preserves "Every audience member had to applaud" accurately?
options: Every audience member could not help to applaud. / could not but applauding.
Every audience member could not help applauding. / could not but applaud.
Every audience member could not help applaud. / could not but to applaud.
No audience member could help not applauding.
questions.explanation: Use 'cannot/could not help + V-ing' OR 'cannot/could not but + Bare V1'.
distractorRationales: Swaps gerund and bare infinitive forms.
Correct: 'could not help + V-ing' and 'could not but + Bare V1'.
Omits '-ing' on first and adds 'to' on second.
questions.grammarRule: 'Must / Have to' transforms negatively to 'cannot help + V-ing' or 'cannot but + Bare V1'.

questions.questionText: Rewrite "If you do not water the potted jasmine, it will wilt" using 'Unless':
options: Unless you do not water the potted jasmine, it will wilt.
Unless you water the potted jasmine, it will wilt.
Unless you will water the potted jasmine, it wilts.
Unless you watered the potted jasmine, it will wilt.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' = 'if... not', so replace 'If you do not water' cleanly with 'Unless you water'.
questions.grammarRule: 'If + S + do/does not + V1' = 'Unless + S + V1'.

questions.subtopicTitle: As soon as → No sooner ... than
questions.questionText: Transform accurately: "As soon as the curtain rose, the hall grew silent."
options: No sooner the curtain rose than the hall grew silent.
No sooner did the curtain rise than the hall grew silent.
No sooner had the curtain risen when the hall grew silent.
No sooner did the curtain rose than the hall grew silent.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' at the start requires auxiliary inversion ('did the curtain rise' OR 'had the curtain risen') followed strictly by 'than'.
distractorRationales: Correct: 'No sooner did + S + V1 ... than'.
questions.grammarRule: Transform 'As soon as...' into 'No sooner did/had + S + verb ... than...'.

questions.subtopicTitle: Part of speech: Verb to Noun
questions.storyContext: Maharaj Vakya opens the final chamber seal.
questions.questionText: Transform "Detective Ira decided quickly" so that 'decided' becomes a NOUN without changing the core meaning:
options: Detective Ira made a quick decision.
Detective Ira was decisive quickly.
Detective Ira quickly decides.
Detective Ira's quickly decision happened.
questions.explanation: 'Decided' (Verb) + 'quickly' (Adverb) converts smoothly to 'made a quick decision' (Verb 'made' + Adjective 'quick' + Noun 'decision').
distractorRationales: Correct: transforms verb to noun 'decision' and adverb to adjective 'quick'.
'Decisive' is an adjective, not a noun.
questions.grammarRule: When changing a verb to its noun form, pair it with a light verb ('make a decision', 'take pride') and shift adverbs to adjectives.
